extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and video game developers interested in copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal criteria and tests used to evaluate copyright infringement claims involving video games—covers fixation, idea-expression distinction, substantial similarity, abstraction test, preliminary injunction standards, and what elements of a game are protectable. Focused on applying these principles to determine whether a game is an infringing 'clone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixation / audiovisual work requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a video game's graphics count as a 'fixed' audiovisual work—an essential first step for copyright protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the time of Atari v. Philips, courts had to decide whether video game graphics constituted a fixed work; courts consistently ruled for plaintiffs that copyright protected games as audiovisual works (more so than the underlying code). This is described as an essential first step for granting copyright protection to a game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea–expression distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects a work's particular expression, not the underlying ideas; broad game concepts are unprotectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply the idea-expression distinction (e.g., Nichols v. Universal Pictures Corp.) to exclude generic elements such as the idea of opponents chasing a character through a maze, scoring, dots, or tunnel exits from protection. Atari v. Amusement World is cited as a case where features were held unprotected as essential to the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction test (Nichols-derived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the abstractions/abstraction test to separate protectable expression from unprotectable ideas across levels of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Harlington Wood applied the abstraction test from Nichols to determine which audiovisual elements of Pac-Man were protectable expression. The test guides courts in identifying which specific expressive features (e.g., character design) may be copyrighted while leaving underlying ideas free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access plus substantial similarity to prove copying
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove copying, plaintiffs must show the defendant had access to the work and that the works are substantially similar in protected elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At trial the issue was whether Philips had access (not contested here) and whether K.C. Munchkin was substantially similar to the legally protected parts of Pac-Man. The combination of access and substantial similarity is the standard route to proving copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial similarity / ordinary observer test
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an ordinary observer would perceive that the defendant copied protected elements; exact reproduction is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appeals court concluded an 'ordinary observer' would see that Munchkin copied Pac-Man. The opinion states 'it is enough that substantial parts were lifted; no plagiarist can excuse the wrong by showing how much of his work he did not pirate.' Case law suggests moderate degrees of similarity may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected vs unprotected elements (non-essential vs essential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which elements of a game are expressive and protectable (non-essential details like character design) versus which are essential to the idea (game mechanics) and unprotectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court held Atari could not prevent others from making any maze-chase game (the idea) but could prevent games that copied expressive features such as the Pac-Man 'gobbler' character and ghost designs. Examples: character appearance and monster design protected; scoring mechanics and dots as generic features are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of success standard for preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction must show a likelihood of success at trial (among other factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court denied Atari's preliminary injunction motion for lack of demonstrated likelihood of success; the appeals court reversed, finding Atari likely to succeed and ordered a preliminary injunction barring sales of Munchkin pending resolution. This standard controls whether sales can be halted pre-trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of remedy: injunction versus tailored remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether to issue a full injunction halting sales or a narrower remedy (e.g., removing infringing expression) to avoid an 'all-or-nothing' outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators (University of Pennsylvania Law Review) warned that injunctions risk an 'all-or-nothing' approach and suggested alternative remedies where a defendant removes infringing expression rather than blocking the entire product. Courts may weigh competitive and innovation impacts when choosing remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of copying from contemporaneous marketing and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Use contemporaneous advertisements, developer statements, and market behavior as evidence bearing on copying and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Atari v. Philips, Philips' advertising openly compared Munchkin to Pac-Man and private investigators found retailers making comparisons—factual patterns that supported the inference of copying or intent to take advantage of Pac-Man's popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of 'look and feel' and expressive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may protect a game's particular expressive content or 'look and feel,' but application is contested and varies by case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atari v. Philips established that expressive content in video games can be protected, including certain visual designs. Later cases produced conflicting rulings (e.g., Data East v. Epyx found no infringement; Tetris v. Xio found infringement), illustrating uncertainty about the extent of 'look and feel' protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of similarity required: moderate similarity may suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a moderate degree of similarity between protected elements may be sufficient to support an infringement claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Emory Law Journal noted that 'only a moderate degree of similarity need be required' to support infringement. The appeals court's wording in Atari v. Philips supports that substantial copying does not require verbatim copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative protection of audiovisual expression versus underlying code
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts historically emphasized copyright protection for audiovisual expression over protection for underlying source code, although both may be protectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early video game cases focused on whether audiovisual elements were fixed and protected; courts were more consistent in treating graphics as protectable audiovisual works while treating underlying code as a separate consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy consideration: chilling effects on competition and small developers
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying copyright protection and remedies, consider potential chilling effects on competition and whether enforcement disproportionately burdens smaller creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators observed that aggressive enforcement (e.g., injunctions) could discourage smaller companies from producing games that resemble existing ones if they cannot afford litigation—an equity/policy concern to weigh alongside legal merits.
